config.title: Build long task profiler using performance API

intro.title: Build long task profiler using performance API
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple profiler that detects and logs long-running tasks in a web application using the Performance API. You will learn how to use the PerformanceObserver interface to monitor performance entries and identify tasks that block the main thread. The core programming concepts involved include event listeners, callbacks, and basic conditionals to filter performance data. By the end, you'll have a working tool that helps you understand and improve your app's responsiveness.
intro.usecase: Long task profiling is essential for optimizing performance in data-intensive web applications like analytics dashboards and financial platforms. Developers use the Performance API to identify JavaScript execution bottlenecks that cause UI freezes in interactive elements such as complex data tables, real-time charts, and multi-step forms. By monitoring long tasks, teams can improve responsiveness in products like Google Analytics, trading interfaces, or collaborative editing tools where smooth user interaction is critical. This pattern helps maintain 60fps rendering and meet Core Web Vitals thresholds for better user retention and SEO rankings.

objectives: Initialize a PerformanceObserver to monitor long tasks
Configure the observer to detect tasks exceeding 50ms threshold
Implement a callback function to process long task entries
Construct a display function to render performance data in the DOM
Integrate the observer with event handlers for user interaction
Manipulate the observer lifecycle to start and stop monitoring
Apply the profiler to identify performance bottlenecks in sample code

steps.title: Import the Performance Observer API
steps.instruction: Import the PerformanceObserver and performance APIs from the global window object.
steps.hint: You can access these APIs directly from the global window object. No package installation is needed.
steps.seedCode: // Import PerformanceObserver and performance from window object
steps.expectedOutcome: The PerformanceObserver and performance APIs are now accessible for monitoring long tasks.
successCriteria: PerformanceObserver and performance are imported from the window object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the Performance Observer API. This gives you access to browser performance monitoring capabilities.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both PerformanceObserver and performance from the window object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import both PerformanceObserver and performance from the window object to monitor long tasks.

steps.title: Create the main profiler function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'startLongTaskProfiler' that will initialize the performance observer. The function should be empty for now.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Just define the function with the correct name.
steps.seedCode:
// Import PerformanceObserver and performance from window object

// Create the startLongTaskProfiler function here
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named startLongTaskProfiler is defined and ready to contain the performance observer initialization logic.
successCriteria: The startLongTaskProfiler function is defined with the correct name and an empty body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the main profiler function. This will serve as the entry point for our long task monitoring system.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function is named exactly 'startLongTaskProfiler' and has a proper function body.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition is missing or incorrect. Please create a function named 'startLongTaskProfiler' with an empty body.

steps.title: Initialize an empty array to store long tasks
steps.instruction: Inside the startLongTaskProfiler function, declare a variable named 'longTasks' and initialize it as an empty array.
steps.hint: Use 'let' or 'const' to declare the variable, then assign it an empty array [].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating an array to store data
let collectedData = [];
steps.expectedOutcome: The function now contains a variable 'longTasks' that is an empty array, ready to store captured long task data.
successCriteria: The startLongTaskProfiler function contains a variable named 'longTasks' initialized as an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created storage for the long tasks. The empty array is ready to hold performance data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared a variable named 'longTasks' and set it to an empty array [] inside the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the startLongTaskProfiler function, create a variable called 'longTasks' and assign it an empty array.

steps.title: Create the Performance Observer instance
steps.instruction: Inside the startLongTaskProfiler function, create a new PerformanceObserver instance that will monitor long tasks. Pass a callback function that receives entries as its parameter.
steps.hint: Use 'new PerformanceObserver()' with a callback function that takes an 'entries' parameter. The callback will handle the observed performance entries.
steps.expectedOutcome: The startLongTaskProfiler function now contains a PerformanceObserver instance ready to monitor long tasks.
successCriteria: A PerformanceObserver instance is created inside startLongTaskProfiler with a callback function that receives entries.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the PerformanceObserver instance that will monitor long tasks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're creating a new PerformanceObserver with a callback function that takes 'entries' as a parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PerformanceObserver instance wasn't created correctly. Remember to use 'new PerformanceObserver()' with a callback function inside startLongTaskProfiler.

steps.title: Define the observer callback function
steps.instruction: Inside the PerformanceObserver constructor, define the callback function that will process the observed long task entries.
steps.hint: The callback function receives a list of entries. You'll need to loop through them in the next step.
steps.expectedOutcome: The PerformanceObserver now has a callback function defined, ready to process long task entries.
successCriteria: The PerformanceObserver constructor includes a callback function parameter that receives 'list'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined the observer callback function. This function will be called whenever new long tasks are detected.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've added the callback function inside the PerformanceObserver constructor.
steps.feedbackWrong: The observer callback function isn't properly defined. Check that you've added it as a parameter to the PerformanceObserver constructor.

steps.title: Configure the observer to watch for long tasks
steps.instruction: Call the observer.observe() method inside the startLongTaskProfiler function to start monitoring for long tasks. Pass it the configuration object { entryTypes: ['longtask'] }.
steps.hint: The observe method tells the PerformanceObserver what type of entries to watch for. Use the exact entry type 'longtask'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The observer is configured to start monitoring for long task performance entries.
successCriteria: observer.observe() is called with the configuration object { entryTypes: ['longtask'] } inside the function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The observer is now configured to watch for long tasks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling observer.observe() with the exact configuration { entryTypes: ['longtask'] }.
steps.feedbackWrong: The observer needs to be configured to watch for long tasks. Call observer.observe({ entryTypes: ['longtask'] }) inside the function.

steps.title: Return the longTasks array from the function
steps.instruction: Inside the startLongTaskProfiler function, add a return statement that returns the longTasks array so the collected data can be accessed.
steps.hint: Use the 'return' keyword followed by the array variable name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The startLongTaskProfiler function now returns the longTasks array, making the collected long task data accessible when the function is called.
successCriteria: The function includes a return statement that returns the longTasks array variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned the longTasks array from the function, allowing the profiler data to be accessed by other parts of your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning the correct variable (longTasks) and that the return statement is placed inside the function body.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't yet return the longTasks array. Add a return statement with the array variable name before the function ends.

steps.title: Create a function to simulate long tasks
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'simulateLongTask' that performs CPU-intensive work for at least 50ms. Place this function after your existing startLongTaskProfiler function.
steps.hint: You can create a function that runs a loop or performs heavy calculations to simulate a long task. Use a while loop with Date.now() to block the main thread for a specified duration.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named simulateLongTask is added that blocks the main thread for at least 50ms to simulate a long task.
successCriteria: The simulateLongTask function exists and contains a busy loop or heavy calculation that runs for at least 50ms.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a function to simulate long tasks, which will help test your profiler.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it performs CPU-intensive work for at least 50ms to properly simulate a long task.
steps.feedbackWrong: The simulateLongTask function is missing or doesn't simulate a long task. Try creating a function that blocks the main thread for at least 50ms.

steps.title: Initialize the profiler and capture data
steps.instruction: Call the startLongTaskProfiler() function to begin monitoring long tasks, then call simulateLongTask() to generate test data.
steps.hint: You'll need to call both functions sequentially. Place these calls after the function definitions in your code.
steps.expectedOutcome: The profiler will be initialized and begin monitoring for long tasks, while the simulateLongTask function will create test data for observation.
successCriteria: Both startLongTaskProfiler() and simulateLongTask() are called in the code.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the profiler and triggered test long tasks. The profiler is now actively monitoring for performance events.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling both functions: startLongTaskProfiler() to begin monitoring and simulateLongTask() to generate test data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The profiler needs to be started and test data needs to be generated. Call both startLongTaskProfiler() and simulateLongTask() functions.

steps.title: Display the captured long task data
steps.instruction: Log the longTasks array to the console to see the captured performance entries.
steps.hint: Use console.log() inside the startLongTaskProfiler function after returning the array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The long task data collected by the profiler will be visible in the browser's developer console.
successCriteria: The longTasks array is logged to the console using console.log().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully logged the long task data to the console. Now you can see the performance entries captured by your profiler.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're logging the longTasks array directly using console.log().
steps.feedbackWrong: The long task data isn't being logged to the console. Add a console.log() statement to display the longTasks array.
